title: Valiant-for-Truth crosses the river
hookLine: at the end of Pilgrim's Progress, Valiant-for-Truth crosses the river and all the trumpets sound
carry: death is a crossing, with a welcome beyond
tomorrow: he went to a meeting unwillingly. what happened at a quarter to nine?

lines: HE GIVES THE SWORD, KEEPS THE SCARS.
cards: Airport arrivals: the balloons, the hand-lettered signs, somebody running before the doors fully open. A homecoming is loud. So why does a book about a long, hard walk end with trumpets?
John Bunyan's Pilgrim's Progress closes at a river, and the river is death. You'd expect a hush.
Instead, there's a puzzle in the last scene: a man hands over his sword, keeps his scars, walks into the water, and the far bank erupts.

teach.b: The man is Mr. Valiant-for-Truth, a pilgrim who has fought hard all the way. When word comes that it's his time, he gives his things away.
"My sword I give to him that shall succeed me in my pilgrimage." That's the first half of the puzzle: the sword is a tool, and tools go to the next traveler.

teach.h: MY MARKS AND SCARS I CARRY.
teach.b: Then: "My marks and scars I carry with me." Why keep those? Because, he says, they're a witness that he fought the battles of the one who will now reward him.
The scars aren't something to hide on arrival. They're his story, and he brings it. Then friends walk him to the riverside.
As he goes in he says, "Death, where is thy sting?" and as the water rises, "Grave, where is thy victory?" Those are Paul's words, from his letter to the Corinthians.
And then the line Bunyan's readers waited for: "So he passed over, and all the trumpets sounded for him on the other side." So the puzzle solves this way. Bunyan doesn't end the road at a grave.
He ends it at an arrival, and on the far bank somebody has been waiting, trumpets ready.

how: Valiant-for-Truth's farewell is sometimes read at Christian funerals; many churches sing hymns of hope, not only sorrow, as a coffin leaves.

o: Bunyan's last scene: a welcome as a pilgrim crosses over
the start of a battle in an old English war story
a church custom of blowing horns on Easter morning

games.q: at the river — tap the pairs.

s: Valiant-for-Truth gives away his sword and his scars
the sword goes to the next pilgrim. the marks and scars he carries with him.
in Bunyan's story, the river the pilgrims cross is death
and the welcome on the far bank is the trumpets.
'Death, where is thy sting?' is Bunyan's own line
it's Paul's, from 1 Corinthians 15:55. Valiant says it as he goes in.

games.q: at your great-aunt's funeral, the family asks the band for something joyful as they leave. your cousin whispers that it's disrespectful. what's in Bunyan's ending?
o: trumpets on the far bank: a death told as a welcome home.
silence: Bunyan has the dead mourned without any music.
a stern warning to the living, and no celebration.
games.why: friends walk Valiant to the river, he crosses, and all the trumpets sound for him on the other side. grief and welcome share the scene.

practice: Close your eyes and remember one real welcome: a door opening, your name called out, someone who couldn't wait for you to get there. Stay inside that moment and let the sound of it fill the room.
If you pray, you can let it stand for the far bank in Bunyan's story.

wordCard.voice: The trumpets sounded. Bunyan's last scene: a river crossed, scars kept, and a welcome on the other side.

orig.note: Greek: sting, goad. Paul's word in 1 Corinthians 15:55, the question Valiant asks at the river.

carryVoice: Your line: death is a crossing, with a welcome beyond. In Bunyan, the road ends at an arrival, not a grave. Day 1661, home.
